_note: The printed key gives \(r=45\). The ratio reduces exactly to \(3080(51-r)\): \(r=41\) gives \(3080\times10=30800\) as required, while \(r=45\) gives \(3080\times6=18480\). Both values are admissible in the permutation symbols (\(r+6\le56\), \(r+3\le54\)), so the discrepancy is a genuine key error, not a domain issue.

solution: CROWN has 5 letters and no letter is repeated, so all 5 objects are distinct and all 5 are being arranged (order matters, repetition not allowed). The number of arrangements is \(5! = 120\). \(\therefore\) 120 words

REMAIN has 6 letters, all different, and all are arranged, so the number of words is \(6! = 720\). For dictionary order the letters rank A, E, I, M, N, R. Words beginning with A number \(5! = 120\), so the \(40^{\text{th}}\) word begins with A. Each choice of the second letter gives \(4! = 24\) words: AE... occupies places 1-24 and AI... occupies 25-48, so the required word is the \(16^{\text{th}}\) word of the AI block. Each choice of the third letter gives \(3! = 6\) words: AIE 1-6, AIM 7-12, AIN 13-18, so it is the \(4^{\text{th}}\) word of the AIN block. Each choice of the fourth letter gives \(2! = 2\) words: AINE 1-2, AINM 3-4, so it is the \(2^{\text{nd}}\) word of the AINM block, i.e. AINMRE. \(\therefore\) 720 words, and the \(40^{\text{th}}\) word is AINMRE

A password is an ordered string of three of the 11 symmetric letters, and the three letters are taken to be different (no repetition). So we both choose and arrange: \({}^{11}P_3 = 11\times10\times9 = 990\). \(\therefore\) 990 symmetric three-letter passwords
_note: The stem does not say whether a letter may repeat; the printed key of 990 fixes the intended reading as "no repetition". Had repetition been allowed the count would be \(11^3 = 1331\).

solution: The seven digits 3, 2, 0, 4, 3, 2, 3 are arranged (order matters) but they are not all distinct: 3 occurs three times and 2 occurs twice. All arrangements number \(\frac{7!}{3!\,2!}=\frac{5040}{12}=420\). A number exceeds one million exactly when it is a genuine seven-digit number, i.e. it does not begin with 0. Arrangements beginning with 0 use the other six digits: \(\frac{6!}{3!\,2!}=\frac{720}{12}=60\). So the count is \(420-60=360\). \(\therefore\) 360 numbers

Only which students are selected matters, not any order, and no student repeats. The 4 friends are either all selected or all rejected. If all 4 are in, the other 6 places are filled from the remaining 26 students: \({}^{26}C_6 = 230230\). If all 4 are out, all 10 places are filled from the remaining 26: \({}^{26}C_{10} = 5311735\). The two cases are disjoint, so the total is \(230230 + 5311735 = 5541965\). \(\therefore\) 5541965 selections

A borrowing is a selection of 3 of the 7 books; order does not matter and no book is repeated. Without any restriction there are \({}^{7}C_3 = 35\) choices. The condition forbids exactly those selections that contain Chemistry Part II but not Chemistry Part I: such a selection takes Chemistry Part II together with 2 of the 5 books other than Chemistry Part I, i.e. \({}^{5}C_2 = 10\) selections. Hence the number of allowed selections is \(35 - 10 = 25\). \(\therefore\) 25 ways
_note: The printed key gives 15. That value comes from reading "Chemistry II only if Chemistry I" as a package — take both or neither — which also bars Chemistry I alone: neither book, \({}^{5}C_3 = 10\), plus both books with 1 of the remaining 5, \(5\), total 15. Read strictly, the condition only rules out Chemistry II without Chemistry I, so Chemistry I on its own is permitted and the count is \(35-10=25\). The strict reading is followed here.

solution: Within each group only the selection matters, not the order; and since the three group sizes 7, 10, 13 are all different the groups are distinguishable, so no division by a group-interchange factor is needed. Choose 7 objects, then 10 from the remaining 23, and the last 13 form the third group: \({}^{30}C_7\times{}^{23}C_{10}\times{}^{13}C_{13}=\frac{30!}{7!\,23!}\times\frac{23!}{10!\,13!}=\frac{30!}{7!\,10!\,13!}\). \(\therefore\) the number of ways is \(\frac{30!}{7!\,10!\,13!}\)

For each of the 7 subjects the student independently either secures the minimum or does not, so there are \(2^7 = 128\) possible outcomes. Exactly one of these — securing the minimum in all 7 subjects — is a pass; every other outcome is a fail. Hence the number of ways of failing is \(2^7 - 1 = 128 - 1 = 127\). \(\therefore\) 127 ways

The two groups are distinguishable — one travels by car, the other by train — so a split is fixed once the car group is chosen; only the selection matters, not any order. With at least 3 friends in each group the car group may contain 3, 4, 5 or 6 of the 9 friends. The number of ways is \({}^{9}C_3+{}^{9}C_4+{}^{9}C_5+{}^{9}C_6 = 84+126+126+84 = 420\). \(\therefore\) 420 ways
_note: The printed key stops at \({}^{9}C_3+{}^{9}C_4+{}^{9}C_5 = 336\). Because the car group and the train group are distinguishable, "6 by car and 3 by train" is a different arrangement from "3 by car and 6 by train", so \({}^{9}C_6\) belongs in the sum as well and the correct total is 420. (A count of 336 would be right only if the two groups were interchangeable, which they are not.)

solution: Each of the 12 lamps is switched on or off independently, so there are \(2^{12} = 4096\) states of the hall. The hall is illuminated only if at least one lamp is on, so the single all-off state is excluded: \(2^{12}-1 = 4095\). \(\therefore\) 4095 ways

A quadratic equation \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) requires \(a\ne0\). The three coefficients occupy fixed positions (so the choice is ordered) and repetition is allowed. Hence \(a\) can be chosen in 3 ways (2, 4 or 5, since \(a\ne0\)), while \(b\) and \(c\) can each be chosen in 4 ways: \(3\times4\times4 = 48\). \(\therefore\) 48 quadratic equations

The first two places are fixed as 4 and 5, so those two digits are already used and cannot appear again. The remaining 4 places are filled from the other 8 digits, in order and without repetition: \({}^{8}P_4 = 8\times7\times6\times5 = 1680\). \(\therefore\) 1680 telephone numbers

Each of the 6 questions is either attempted or left out, independently, so the questions attempted form any one of \(2^6 = 64\) subsets. Since the student solves at least one question, the empty subset is excluded: \(2^6 - 1 = 63\). \(\therefore\) 63 ways

Within each group only the selection matters, and since the sizes 8, 7 and 5 are all different the groups are distinguishable, so no division by a group-interchange factor is needed. Choose 8 objects, then 7 from the remaining 12, and the last 5 form the third group: \({}^{20}C_8\times{}^{12}C_7\times{}^{5}C_5=\frac{20!}{8!\,12!}\times\frac{12!}{7!\,5!}=\frac{20!}{8!\,7!\,5!}\). \(\therefore\) the number of ways is \(\frac{20!}{8!\,7!\,5!}\)

A team is a selection of 6 people from the 12 panellists; order does not matter and nobody repeats. Total teams: \({}^{12}C_6 = 924\). Teams with no doctor are formed from the 8 lawyers alone: \({}^{8}C_6 = 28\). Teams with at least one doctor are the rest: \(924 - 28 = 896\). \(\therefore\) 896 ways

A parallelogram is determined by a pair of lines from the first set together with a pair from the second set; the lines in a pair are merely chosen, not ordered. So the count is \({}^{4}C_2\times{}^{5}C_2 = 6\times10 = 60\). \(\therefore\) 60 distinct parallelograms

A line is fixed by an unordered pair of points (the pair AB gives the same line as BA), and since the 12 points lie on a circle no three of them are collinear, so distinct pairs give distinct lines. Hence the number of lines is \({}^{12}C_2 = \frac{12\times11}{2} = 66\). \(\therefore\) 66 lines

A line through D is fixed once its other end point is chosen from the remaining 11 points; the choice is unordered and no point repeats. Hence \({}^{11}C_1 = 11\). \(\therefore\) 11 lines pass through D

A triangle is fixed by an unordered choice of 3 of the 12 points, and as the points lie on a circle no three are collinear, so every such choice really does give a triangle. Hence \({}^{12}C_3 = \frac{12\times11\times10}{3\times2\times1} = 220\). \(\therefore\) 220 triangles
Keep C as one vertex and choose the other two vertices, unordered, from the remaining 11 points: \({}^{11}C_2 = \frac{11\times10}{2} = 55\). \(\therefore\) 55 triangles have C as a vertex
